L37@P0: Abstract
L38@P0: We introduce n(n − 1)/2 natural involutions (“toggles”) on the set S of noncrossing partitions π of size n, along with certain composite operations obtained by
L39@P0: composing these involutions. We show that for many operations T of this kind, a
L40@P0: surprisingly large family of functions f on S (including the function that sends π to
L41@P0: the number of blocks of π) exhibits the homomesy phenomenon: the average of f
L42@P0: over the elements of a T-orbit is the same for all T-orbits. We can apply our method
L43@P0: of proof more broadly to toggle operations back on the collection of independent
L44@P0: sets of certain graphs. We utilize this generalization to prove a theorem about toggling on a family of graphs called “2-cliquish.” More generally, the philosophy of
L45@P0: this “toggle-action,” proposed by Striker, is a popular topic of current and future
L46@P0: research in dynamic algebraic combinatorics.

L49@P1: 1 Introduction
L50@P1: A partition of [n] := {1, 2, . . . , n} is a collection π of disjoint sets B1, B2, . . . , BK with
L51@P1: union [n]. We call the Bi’s “blocks” and write |π| = K. A partition π is noncrossing if
L52@P1: whenever 1 6 i < j < k < ` 6 n, we do not have i and k belonging to one block of π
L53@P1: with j and ` belonging to a different block. (For motivation of the term “noncrossing”,
L54@P1: see the discussion of the linear representation of π below, and the circular representation
L55@P1: in Section 2.) Simion and Ullman [SU91] define an involution λ on the set of noncrossing
L56@P1: partitions of [n] (they call it α) with the property that |π| + |λ(π)| = n + 1. This map is
L57@P1: related to a different operation on noncrossing partitions, the Kreweras complementation
L58@P1: [Kre72], denoted κ. The bijection κ is not an involution but it too satisfies |π| + |κ(π)| =
L59@P1: n+1. The actions κ and λ have very different orbit-structures, but they share the property
L60@P1: that the average of |π| over each orbit is (n + 1)/2. That is, in the terminology of Propp
L61@P1: and Roby [PR15], the statistic π 7→ |π| is homomesic under the actions of κ and λ, or
L62@P1: more specifically, c-mesic with c = (n + 1)/2.
L63@P1: In this paper, we exhibit a large class of actions sharing this homomesy property with
L64@P1: κ and λ. These actions are obtained from the toggle-action philosophy first studied by
L65@P1: Cameron and Fon-Der-Flaass [CFDF95] and more recently by Striker and Williams [SW12]
L66@P1: and Striker [Str16]. This philosophy invites us to act on combinatorial objects via operations obtained as compositions of extremely simple involutions. These involutions (called
L67@P1: toggles) may have many fixed points; indeed, it is usually the case that for any given toggle
L68@P1: operation τ acting on a set S of combinatorial objects being studied, most of the elements
L69@P1: of S are fixed by τ . However, by composing many toggles we obtain a permutation T of
L70@P1: S that mixes S up more than any individual toggle does. Propp and Roby [PR15] add
L71@P1: to this picture the observation that in many cases of interest, T does such a good job of
L72@P1: mixing up S that, for some interesting numerical statistics f on S, the average of f on
L73@P1: each T-orbit is some constant that only depends on f, not what orbit we are in.
L74@P1: In this article, S is the set of noncrossing partitions π of [n] and f(π) is |π| or various
L75@P1: related quantities. To define the sorts of toggles we use, we make use of the linear
L76@P1: representation of noncrossing partitions, as shown in Figure 1. This representation of π
L77@P1: depicts the numbers 1, . . . , n as equally-spaced points on a horizontal line and consists of
L78@P1: arcs above the line joining points i and j whenever i and j are successive elements of the
L79@P1: same block. Formally, the linear representation P of π consists of those pairs (i, j) with
L80@P1: 1 6 i < j 6 n with the property that i and j are in the same block of π but none of
L81@P1: i+1, i+2, . . . , j−1 (the “interior” of the arc (i, j)) are also in that block. The noncrossing
L82@P1: property of the partition guarantees that if two arcs belong to P, then their interiors are

L84@P1: we never see two arcs exhibiting the three forbidden configurations depicted in Figure 2,
L85@P1: called respectively crossing, left-nesting, and right-nesting. Note however that nested arcs

L178@P4: It is clear that each toggle operation is an involution. The object of this paper is to
L179@P4: understand some well-behaved statistics of the toggle group and its action on NC(n). We
L180@P4: define the relevant notions in Section 4. The choice of Wn to denote the toggle group is
L181@P4: motivated by the fact that it is always a quotient of a Coxeter group, which is classically
L182@P4: denoted by W. We will revisit this in Section 3.
L183@P4: It will be helpful for what follows to classify which pairs of toggles do and do not
L184@P4: commute. Any pair of distinct arcs (i, j) and (k, `) can be classified into one of six types
L185@P4: (possibly after swapping (i, j) with (k, `)):
L186@P4: 1. i < j < k < ` (disjoint),
L187@P4: 2. i < k < ` < j (nesting),
L188@P4: 3. i < j = k < ` (m-shaped),
L189@P4: 4. i = k < j < ` (left-nesting),
L190@P4: 5. i < k < j = ` (right-nesting),
L191@P4: 6. i < k < j < ` (crossing).
L192@P4: The type is sufficient to determine whether or not the pair of toggles commutes.
L193@P4: Proposition 2.2. Let τi,j and τk,` be distinct toggles. Then τi,j and τk,` commute if and
L194@P4: only if the arcs (i, j) and (k, `) are disjoint, nesting, or m-shaped.

L196@P4: P = {} be the empty noncrossing partition of [n]. Then τi,j τk,`(π) = {(k, `)}, whereas
L197@P4: τk,`τi,j (π) = {(i, j)}. Thus τi,j and τk,` do not commute.
L198@P4: On the other hand, suppose that (i, j) and (k, `) are disjoint, nested, or m-shaped.
L199@P4: Then adding or removing (i, j) does not interfere with adding or removing (k, `), so τi,j
